ABSTRACT

Taking into account the significance and hurdles of blockchain technology in construction work, the current study examines the potential of blockchain technology in the construction industry and how this disruptive technology could revamp construction projects. Using blockchain to simplify the contractual processes and paperwork associated with these complex projects could save money, free up valuable resources, and accelerate project completion. The blockchain records are tamper-proof, which will help enforce work compliance and discourage potential record fabrication. As a result, it makes sense to begin focusing on blockchain convergence efforts in these sectors and then extend them as the technology improves.

INTRODUCTION

The construction sector in India is expanding rapidly, with a 10% increase predicted over the next five years. It is the country's second-largest source of employment, employing approximately 50 million people. However, in the construction projects, a slew of additional undesirable factors such as design flaws, inadequate design documents and missed deadlines, budget overruns, and regulatory restraints have slowed several projects across the country (Shah & Ghayas, 2022). These factors cause half of all building projects in India to be delayed. Infrastructure projects need the collaboration of several suppliers and contractors, all of whom must be compensated for their efforts. The present invoice and payment method is sluggish, opaque, and prone to fraud. To achieve its $5 trillion economic objective by 2025 and to continue developing at a rapid rate, the government must use cutting-edge technologies in infrastructure construction. The key constraints identified may be considerably reduced by introducing new technologies in safety, transparency, payment processing speed, and sustainability. Blockchain technology has streamlined this process by generating a transparent and immutable record of all transactions and allowing assets to be tracked from manufacturing through distribution or usage by the end user.

Seebacher and Schuritz (2017) define Blockchain as “a distributed database, which is shared among and agreed upon as a peer-to-peer network. It consists of a linked sequence of blocks (a storage unit of the transaction), holding timestamped transactions that are secured by public-key cryptography (i.e., “hash”) and verified by the network community. Once an element is appended to the Blockchain, it cannot be altered, turning a Blockchain into an immutable record of past activity.” In other terms, Blockchain is described as a growing collection of data known as blocks that are connected together via encryption. Each block includes a hash value of the preceding block, a timestamp, and the user of the data records (Wang et al., 2020). A blockchain is often operated as a public ledger by a peer-to-peer community that follows a mechanism for inter-node communication and verifying new blocks. Once recorded, the contents in any specific block cannot be changed retrospectively without affecting all following blocks, which needs network consensus agreement.

Blockchain technology (BCT) has been deployed in a wide range of sectors, including healthcare, manufacturing, and engineering. Because of its potential benefits, blockchain has sparked the curiosity of building researchers. Smart contracts, for example, are being used to facilitate security and privacy, preserve transaction records, and give anonymous information accessibility (Das et al., 2020). Novel blockchains are being used to solve information gaps in the construction supply chain. Blockchain has been integrated with the building information model (BIM) to improve the BIM working environment (Liu et al., 2019). Through the provision of transparent data and a clear communication of requirements and expectations through smart contracts that precisely describe the parameters agreed upon by the participating parties, BCT adoption can be a successful solution for the better management of construction projects.

The use of blockchain technology has the potential to improve project management and finance functions, including bidding, contract management, project planning, risk assessment, and insurance. Additionally, it would significantly shorten the timeframe and costs needed to transfer money for multinational projects from weeks to minutes (Luo et al., 2019). The construction sector may be able to overcome numerous barriers with the use of latest technologies like the “internet of things (IoT), building information modelling (BIM), and artificial intelligence” when combined with Blockchain technology. A framework stressing innovation, success, and sustainability has arisen because BCT platforms are decentralized, cutting superfluous bureaucracy will increase open communications, and BCT application will prevent disagreements based in the digitalization of corporate operating models. Due to upgraded technologies, improved communication technology, a shorter lead time, a better working environment, and higher-quality products, Industry 4.0 technology is essential for manufacturing industries and their long-term survival (Kamble et al., 2018).

Blockchain technologies are widespread, particularly in conservative sectors like the construction industry, which has been sluggish to accept technology innovations to enhance operations and workflows. Nonetheless, numerous solutions have overcome construction industry difficulties with exceptional outcomes. Blockchain-based contracts, smart contracts for transparency and traceability, and enhanced information flow are driving this expansion (Wang et al., 2020). Construction is behind other businesses (Ye et.al., 2018). Researchers must provide construction practitioners with a full analysis of blockchain applications, including their advantages and disadvantages in order to increase blockchain adoption. Blockchain uses in building are poorly understood. This research examines how blockchain technology might enhance construction project workflows and identifies the constructions industry potential, limitations, and issues.

MATERIAL AND METHODOLOGY

The construction industry has always been striving to improve productivity and effectiveness while also seizing the advantages availed by technology advancements. This study investigates the possibilities of blockchain in the construction sector and examines how this digital revolution has the power to disrupt the construction business by boosting the efficiency of procedures and operations. This research paper identifies the function and major elements that drive BCT adoption in construction organisations, as well as the causal links that affect and enable blockchain technology implementation in the construction sector. These influencing elements for BCT acceptance were investigated in order to assure a comprehensive blockchain integration in construction enterprises and projects.

A systematic literature analysis and search methods were employed to filter blockchain-related research publications from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. The research strategy and framework used a holistic approach in which blockchain adoption in the construction industry was based on three fundamental factors: drivers, rationale, and advantages. The conclusions of the study will assist construction stakeholders, businesses, and policymakers in understanding the complexities of the linked aspects that impact blockchain adoption and how to address them. The insights will also help the industry's important stakeholders deploy blockchain and related technology. The article emphasised the need of the construction industry investigating the many functions of BCT in order to measure the actual advantages.

Blockchain Characteristics

Technology breakthroughs have provided the groundwork for information sharing; nevertheless, these technical advancements confront limitations in achieving their needs, such as a lack of safety, transparency, confidence, and connectivity, to mention a few. These difficulties have been solved by a blockchain system. BCT, for example, safeguards data in IoT that is susceptible to hackers by preserving it in blocks indefinitely. (Amanullah at el., 2020). The unique characteristics of BCT that have evolved businesses and their systems are as follows:

Figure 1. Blockchain characteristics

Decentralization

Decentralization transfers authority and responsibility of major government functions from central to sub-national governments including local governments, civil society, and the private sector. A decentralized system is a network whose members can be computing nodes, manufacturing machines, robots, or humans. Every node is a part of the network that copies all blocks. The nodes verify data security in a network whose members are identified by an address (Arashpour et al., 2019). The platform is not administered by a single body. All operations in a widespread peer-to-peer connection are stored in a list of public blocks. No individual has total authority over the system, and each participant has the opportunity to see the data; accessibility is determined by the network's access rights. Because of the high degree of accessibility, all participating nodes check the recorded data; hence, no one can edit a specific document to their advantage. (Wang et al., 2019)

Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) is one of the latest innovations that has received the greatest attention. The widespread use of the cryptocurrency Bitcoin has increased interest in blockchain technology and distributed ledger technology (DLT) in general. A digital asset called a cryptocurrency is made to be a means of trade. Transactions and represented assets are protected against tampering and fraud by the use of encryption protocols (Chohan, 2022).

Consensus

Consensus algorithms create trust amongst unidentified peers in a computing environment and provide dependability in the Blockchain network, The consensus process serves as the foundational element of a blockchain network, ensuring that in such trustless settings, all participants concur on the network's state. The consensus method also controls the network's other functions, like transaction addition and motivating players to act ethically. Due to delay in connection or classical failures, nodes inside a blockchain may be defective, engaging in arbitrary or hostile behaviour, or holding inaccurate information. The consensus mechanism of a blockchain network assures that in such thrustless contexts, all participants agree on the network's state.

Blockchain Immutability

Immutability, often known as irreversibility, is a basic blockchain attribute resulting from the fact that operations cannot be altered or removed after they have been properly authenticated and stored in the blockchain. This attribute is the result of cryptographically linked blocks concatenated together with the hash algorithm of the previous (parent) block. Each block, in specifically, carries a reference to the prior block by adding a hash function of the transaction information in the previous block in its header. This cryptographic hash is calculated using a Merkle tree on all of the block's transactions.

Security

By enabling only approved stakeholders to transmit information, the BCT encrypted protocol ensures the validity of data and participants. In this aspect, the protocol employs a “one-way” hash function to turn any length input into a user defined output termed hash value. When a new transaction has been made, cryptography connects it to previous ones; this is how blockchain technologies are resilient and secure. Because an encrypted hash function encrypts data, attackers cannot foresee the starting data and, as a result, cannot modify or tamper with it (Fang et al., 2020).

Transparency

Blockchain has the ability to create a professional chain of evidence. This capacity promotes traceability and openness in the data sharing process (Kshetri, 2017). Transparency contributes to being conscious of the current state of the record. Transparency makes people understand the ledger's functioning. Furthermore, because various blockchain technologies allow users to search entries on a repository, members may track data with verifiable timestamps. A centralized repository cannot provide a consistent, safe, and transparent network for managing high-quality data.

Privacy

The term “privacy” in blockchain networks refers to two aspects: user privacy and transaction data privacy. The following are the two forms of transaction privacy in blockchains:

User Privacy (Anonymity): the capacity to change a blockchain user's genuine identity into one that cannot be recognized, while also assuring that the original identity remains unattainable. This is more usually referred to as anonymity. It hides the user's true identity by disguising the user's real network address with a computer-generated address. By concealing the details of an operation, blockchain data privacy is preserved. Confidential information is also known as privacy. At the simplest basic level, the data contents of a transaction are normally encrypted to ensure network secrecy. Maintaining data confidentiality protects transaction contents against unauthorised access, tampering, and alteration.

THE ROLE OF BCT CHARACTERISTICS IN ADDRESSING CONSTRUCTION ISSUES

Blockchain offers various possible applications in the early stages of an infrastructure project. Smart contracts and cryptocurrencies are the most apparent outcomes of implementing blockchain into a building project during the design stage. When the stages of a design process (identification, planning, purchase, execution status, and so on) are transferred to blockchain, every member in the chain validates and updates credible project information to work with. This strategy can reduce uncertainty, boost productivity, and minimize errors. The person who generated the block contains information on the identity and it may also identify who is responsible for specific information. Smart contracts can be utilized to link internal functions to a BIM model in order to increase supply chain transaction efficiency; to confirm important process events like as permitting and inspections; to enable financial transactions; to confirm modification orders; and to provide notice. The end result is a clear record of a project's procedure as well as the structure's as-built condition.

Major delays and disagreements in Indian construction projects are related with payment claim resolution, documentation, and stakeholder participation. BCT can handle a wide range of system difficulties by providing decentralisation, security, and transparency. Globally, capital construction activities have a highly fragmented, dispersed, and complicated supply chain. For example, at the height of its development, the Burj Khalifa employed nearly 12,000 employees from more than 100 nations. Massive effort and resources are required to manage such a large supply chain and keep track of work in progress, schedule, cost, and payments.

Figure 2 depicts the relationship between BCT features and related responsibilities and payment, collaboration, and documentation traceability issues in construction.

Figure 2. Blockchain in construction

Globally, the supply chain for capital building operations is highly unstable, scattered, and complex. During the peak of its construction, the Burj Khalifa employed almost 12,000 workers from more than 100 countries. To handle such a broad distribution network and maintain records of work in progress, scheduling, cost, and payments requires massive effort and resources. In addition to these challenges, construction projects encounter a range of mistakes, delays, and accidents at different phases and to varying degrees. In the construction industry, irresponsibility has been an issue for decades, and with profit margins so low, firms are searching for ways to minimise costs and avoid liability for the resulting tragedies. These are the key “pain points” and areas where blockchain technology might be utilised to make the process more effective, transparent, and responsible for all project participants.

Progress in Collaborations

Construction has always been a team effort including a large or small number of people. Communication technology has had a tremendous influence on the relationships of individuals connected throughout history. Construction projects are complex where great number of stakeholders are involved in the project leads to fragmentation issues among the professionals and organisations. Existing construction methods, on the other hand, face several issues relating to trust, knowledge transfer, and operational processes (Wang at al., 2017).

Figure 3. Blockchain collaborative project system

However, distributed ledger technology, among other things, offers trust, data integrity, accuracy, confidentiality, and transparency, allowing management difficulties to be resolved. Construction designs, for example, might be provided at various stages, and all parties must be notified. However, because the stakeholders operate in distinct companies, numerous challenges may occur, such as identifying the most recent set of drawings, who issued the most recent drawing, whether it was included with the architectural/structural/service designs, and so on. All of these concerns may be overcome by using a blockchain system with smart contracts, since the most recent information can be updated and made available to the appropriate parties.

Blockchain technology enables people to securely interact, organise, and transact. As a result, BCT promotes user cooperation by increasing data sharing and decreasing hierarchy. key stakeholder of a construction project is part of a blockchain empowered network. In this way the governance of the network is based on the consensus and agreement of all stakeholders. Each participant would have their own, but same, copy of the blockchain, which includes every interaction and transaction between the parties. Interactions and payments are documented, tamper-proof, and cryptographically signed regardless of whether this information is private or completely contained for each stakeholder. This produces an easily traceable record of every commercial transaction of all parties in the past. In this manner, the complexity of project control and the risk associated with it might be greatly decreased, possibly by as much as the cost of administration. To improve operational efficiencies and traceability, cryptographic protocols (self-executing conditions that may be integrated in blockchain-based systems) can be used. With such a system, trust and collaboration among all players would be greatly enhanced.

Having Equal Right to Share Ideas

BCT fosters a culture of collaboration in which duties are clearly defined and risks/rewards are shared among participants. Smart contracts manage access responsibility and reward users and application owners for providing user data. By combining the security and immutability of data kept in the blockchain with the special characteristics of two prominent blockchains—MultiChain and Ethereum—participants may combine their advantages: adequate data storage and data sharing, as well as smart contracts for access control mechanisms. As a result, our new platform overcomes the inadequacies of traditional centralised user models employed by internet enterprises, which have security flaws, lack accountability, and deprive users of ownership, control, and incentives for data sharing. BCT defines process routes in each project, fostering trust and collaboration among stakeholders (Nawar & Ravindran, 2019). Because construction projects have a competitive atmosphere, BCT avoids unhealthy competitiveness among participants by granting equal rights to input data and equal standing in consensus decision making. In general, a blockchain is utilised to eliminate weak and distrusting interactions in physical areas, hence altering interactions in organisations.

Reducing Bureaucracy and Corruption

Building projects are participatory processes that require less red tape and greater openness. Due to knowledge asymmetry, players in traditional contracts shift away from immediate contractual arrangements and toward more and more expensive modes of engagement. BCT transforms a hierarchical organisation into a productive network by providing project stakeholders with a distributed blockchain and up-to-date information. This network results in a transparent interaction and awareness of the state of the site. Financial intermediaries can significantly decrease information asymmetry because they are more accessible and self-executed, which means that once ascertained and in operation, their information is available to all parties. If one of them is a public organisation, the information about the contracts is presumed to be available to the entire society. Furthermore, contracts cannot be deceptively amended, which helps to the contracts' promises and claims while also reducing asymmetric knowledge. Smart Contracts are self-contained and perform all actions without the assistance or intervention of a service provider, providing unrivalled transparency, enhancing efficiency, and reducing the possibility of malpractice in construction. Open communication is established for subcontractors, general contractors, inspectors, and other stakeholders, allowing persons to provide and access information in a systematic method (Lu et al., 2021).

Automation With Smart Contracts

Automation using smart contracts is a huge benefit, especially for business owners and executives. Smart Contracts shorten payment times, enable rapid payments, and automate payment processes. When developing smart contracts, be sure to include all of the payment conditions. When the required credentials are satisfied, the individual is automatically compensated. Ethereum smart contracts allow safe data exchange and high-integrity storage information (Gürsoy et al., 2020). One of the earliest blockchain-based apps, the Ethereum platform, allowed computer instructions to be performed on the blockchain. A smart contract is a major invention that has been revitalised by distributed ledger technology. Smart contracts, like conventional contracts, may set rules and automatically enforce them through programming. Smart contracts are inherently irreversible and cannot be erased by default. A smart contract's terms are expressed in a computer language that is also human-readable. When the established prerequisites in a digital contract are satisfied, the contract's provisions are automatically carried out (Allen, 2018).

Funding Management

Most building projects need significant investment from investors, particularly historic structures that serve as vital landmarks for a country. As a result, blockchain-based crowdfunding provides a fantastic chance for project clients to launch a secure platform to seek funds for their projects. The blockchain crowdfunding platforms are peer-to-peer fundraising platforms that potentially replace the requirement for traditional capital finance to start an enterprise (Swan, 2015). This is achievable through the development of own digital currencies and the sale of “cryptographic shares” to early backers. The blockchain crowdfunding platforms also provide investors and clients with trust because the usage of funds is completely transparent with the decentralized blockchain. The consequent outflow from the blockchain ledger may be used to trace the spending of project budgets. Furthermore, due to the decentralised nature of blockchain technology, all financing (outflow and inflow) financial transactions are unchangeable.

Development of Payment Systems

Blockchain innovations have energised smart contracts and payment systems in order to improve financial flows. Every precise transaction data on a cryptography network may be stored on a single encrypted digital gateway. As a result, it offers users with a protected site while also increasing execution speed (Gao et al., 2018). thus, the contractual conflicts and payment issues can be overcome.

Improving Cash Flow

Using a fictitious contract between an employer and a contractor as an example the execution of the contractual obligation can be eased by a blockchain-based consensus mechanism (Khan et al., 2018). The funds are restricted until delivery once the employer deposits a certain amount into the network at the start of the project. When a project is finished, it is ready for distribution, and the blockchain stores details like the time the job was delivered. An automated payment is issued when the supplied job's quality has been verified. However, neither client nor the programmer who wrote the algorithms may alter the contract or postpone payment by relying on the identity codes. Traditional auditing schemes may have restrictions on clients' pay-as-you-go service due to conditions like upfront payment. So, researchers created a system where a cloud service provider (CSP) and data owners manage a fair payment smart contract. CSP gives documentation proving its ownership of the data but is not paid until the verification is successful. The lack of confidence between the buyer and seller is a problem in conventional payment systems; a smart contract built on blockchain can address the issue. Luo et al. (2019) used a blockchain-based smart contract to tackle construction payment issues. This technique formalises parties, their relationships, transaction sequences, and building contract clauses into smart contract code. Automation triggers interim payments following consensus.

A consensus mechanism verifies payment applications from authorised participants. Then, the blockchain ledger stores the application unaltered. The system will record any changes to recorded data. The agreement is issued to stakeholders after transaction confirmation. Hence, system security may be ensured without bank systems (Wang et al., 2017) With an immutable system, audit trails may be used to determine who is at fault for a late payment, whether it was the customer who delayed the payment permission (without legitimate reason) or the contractor who was late with the progress invoices. Thus, a paradigm of searchable encryption that relies on the combination of blockchain technology and searchable symmetric encryption is necessary (Li et al., 2019). This reasonable plan accomplishes a few of things. First, it finds the variance to identify erroneous results. As a second benefit, the blockchain's payment method protects the rights of all participants.

the potential blockchain-based applications involve different construction stages, from design and construction to maintenance. Various project management areas, including cost management, asset management, contract management.

Improvement in Documentation

The validity and reliability of construction quality documentation is critical to establishing confidence. So that all authorized individuals have access to legitimate data, approvals about the quality of raw materials and products, as well as the quality and amount of work progress, can be kept in the blockchain. Uncertainty arises in an insecure centralised system when participants are unaware of the state of the project and the activities of other stakeholders; this provides participants with an opening to exonerate themselves. During disagreements, an opportunistic participant might intentionally prevent other users from using the system. In addition, if the paperwork isn't clear, it might derail any attempts to settle the disagreement without going to court (Gürsoy et al., 2020). As blockchain records cannot be altered after they have been created, this technology may be used to ensure that all work is done in accordance with regulations and prevent any record forgeries. By increasing the safety and openness of document management systems, blockchain technology offers a solution to these problems.

Strengthening Security

BCT's primary use case is in the administration of databases with accurate record presentations. Having easy access to data is critical in such systems, but ensuring that data is secure against manipulation is also important. In order to do this, Sheng et al. (2020) suggested a blockchain-based system. They came up with a method to boost the quality of project data and gave it the catchy moniker “the product organisation process (POP)”. In order to facilitate online cooperation between contractors, employers, consultants, and subcontractors, this framework provides a set of guidelines. They have joined forces by agreeing to work together on a project and by taking part in the POP quality Chain. The procedure is initiated once the asset owner generates a high-quality information document within the framework. The administrative team and the contractors work together to guarantee that the framework is implemented in all projects only once permission is granted to do so. A uniform, safe, and decentralised architecture provides high-quality information management for the accepted protocol. All parties involved in the project have access to a wealth of reliable data thanks to the framework.

Adding Transparency

The credibility and shared understanding that come from open communication are crucial in the conflict resolution process. Due to the lack of openness in centralised data management, a decentralised system is required to provide a shared, immutable, and auditable ledger of all transactions (Dubovitskaya et al., 2017). According to previous studies, blockchain smart contracts might help bring about complete transparency across the whole lifetime. An outside party initiates the workflow by making a networked request that specifies the document number, document verification, the next party, and the due date. Incorrect paperwork is the reason for the request. The architect then evaluates the submitted materials in order to evaluate the claim and reply to the contractor. Blockchain technology makes it possible to track who did what and when in any given workflow. As a result, the process may be seen at any time, and the records can be consulted in the event of a disagreement (Pradeep et al., 2021).

Cost Effective

Blockchain is a new disruptive technology that may increase transparency, lower transaction costs, ensure the safety of financial transactions, and streamline operational procedures. Court proceedings using smart contracts were far lower, saving both time and money. The majority of clients in today's construction business conduct financial and real estate transactions through centralised middlemen like banks and brokers. These middlemen collect fees from their customers in exchange for their services. Yet, the implementation of Blockchain technology in the building sector allows customers to avoid these middlemen and save money on transaction fees (Current, 2017). Project managers may have more influence over the budget and more effectively manage costs by integrating blockchain technology with BIM during the preconstruction phase. Quantity take-off (QTO) based on building information modelling (BIM) and linked to blockchain and smart contract for cost control and payment increased the security and privacy of critical cost data, as did a series of studies that used blockchain and smart contracts to facilitate cost management and trigger automated payment (Ye et al., 2022).

LIMITATIONS OF BLOCKCHAIN IN CONSTRUCTIONS

While blockchain technology has the potential to revolutionize the construction industry, it also has some limitations:

Scalability

The construction industry involves large-scale projects that generate significant amounts of data. Blockchain technology can be slow and inefficient when it comes to processing large volumes of data, which can limit its effectiveness in the construction industry. Blockchain technology can be slow and inefficient, particularly when it comes to processing large volumes of transactions. As more users join the network and more transactions are added to the blockchain, the network can become congested and slow.

Limited Adoption

The construction industry is known to be slow in adopting new technologies, and blockchain is no exception. Many construction firms are still unfamiliar with blockchain technology and are hesitant to invest in it. As mentioned earlier, different blockchain platforms often use different standards and protocols, which can make it difficult for them to interoperate. This can make it challenging for construction firms to collaborate effectively and share data across different platforms.

Figure 4. Limitations of blockchain in constructions

Complexity

Blockchain technology is complex and requires specialized knowledge to implement and manage. This can make it challenging for construction firms to adopt and utilize the technology effectively.

Cost

Implementing blockchain technology can be expensive, particularly for smaller construction firms that may not have the resources to invest in the technology.

Security Risks

While blockchain technology is often touted as being highly secure, it is not completely immune to attacks. In particular, 51% attacks, where a single entity controls more than 50% of the network’s computational power, can pose a serious threat to the integrity of the blockchain. While blockchain transactions are public and transparent, the underlying technology does not provide complete anonymity or privacy. In the construction industry, this can be a concern for companies that want to protect confidential project data.

Energy Consumption

Blockchain technology requires significant amounts of energy to operate. The process of verifying transactions through mining requires vast amounts of computational power and consumes a lot of electricity.

Lack of Regulation

Blockchain technology is still largely unregulated, which can create legal and security issues. The decentralized nature of blockchain networks can also make it difficult to hold individuals or organizations accountable for fraudulent or illegal activities. Blockchain regulation is important for several reasons. One of the main reasons is to protect consumers from fraud and other financial crimes. Cryptocurrencies, a relatively new and largely unregulated asset class, have been vulnerable to scams and other illicit activity. By establishing rules and standards regulators can help reduce the risk of such activities and protect consumers from financial harm.

CONCLUSION

This study provides consolidated both quantitative and qualitative data to provide a deeper understanding of how distributed ledger technology potentially disrupt the construction industry. The application of blockchain in construction can bring about significant benefits, such as improved supply chain management, project management, smart contracts, and asset management. Blockchain technology can provide a transparent, secure, and efficient platform for all stakeholders involved in a construction project, reducing the risk of fraud, improving collaboration, and increasing accountability.

Blockchain technology is still in its early stages in the construction business and is currently in its exploration phase. The functions and possibilities of blockchain use in the construction firms, on the other hand, should not be underestimated. The potential applications of blockchain in the construction sector have been discovered, and these include contract administration, Building Information Modelling (BIM) systems, Electronic Document Management (EDM), property maintenance, supply chain management, and fund management. The decentralised, fully independent, peer-to-peer, and irrevocable record properties of blockchain boost work productivity, save time and money, and stimulate worldwide collaboration in the construction business. Business procedures and administrative operations may be automated using block chain-based smart contracts to boost efficiency and ensure that they always adhere to the contractual conditions. This can result in significant cost savings in construction and better project cost control. Blockchain can simplify the procurement process and reduce the fragmentation and complication of huge projects. The source of the materials has the potential to reduce waste and drive quality of products and services forward with high responsibility. These tools can increase predictability not just in procurement, but also in total project delivery.

Despite the foregoing, there are still numerous steps that must be performed before we can declare that Blockchain is an essential element of the construction process. One of the major obstacles of blockchain implementation in the construction sector is the government's approach to regulating blockchain technology in the nations themselves, namely the regulation of initial coin offerings (ICO), which are mostly utilised for project fundraising. Several nations have outlawed the use of blockchain technology in their countries due to the negative consequences of blockchain activities (such as criminal activity and unrestrained currency and financial outflow), whereas others have applied and developed more of the potentials of blockchain technology in their countries. However, another barrier to blockchain deployment in the construction industry is the industry's delayed acceptance of technology in comparison to other industries.

ABSTRACT

Blockchain is a new technology that allows for the decentralized and transactional sharing of data across a large network of untrusted participants. It allows for new types of distributed software architectures. Although the technology was initially used primarily in digital currency, it is a promising technology in other areas as well. This chapter provides a simplified introduction to blockchain technology. It also discusses how blockchain technology can be used in some business processes in the retail sector to greatly benefit both customers and retailers. This chapter specifically discusses issues of retail supply chain management (SCM) and how blockchain technology is transitioning the retail supply chain management. The chapter discusses the market trend in blockchain adoption as well as some of the challenges.

INTRODUCTION

Blockchain is a digital system of transaction and data recording. It serves as a public ledger of shared digital events or transactions over a sizable network of unreliable individuals, or as a distributed database of records. Any industry that has previously depended on third-party verification is now disrupted by its removal. The majority of system members are supposed to confirm each transaction in the public ledger. Because information entered is immutable, it can never be erased.

Blockchain has drawn interest from a variety of sectors besides the financial one and has applications in the manufacturing, healthcare, consumer products, public sector, food business, and many more. Blockchain might have revolutionary uses in the retail supply chain.

Blockchain has been characterised, even in its infancy, as a shared ledger in which all financial transactions are recorded, so avoiding the inaccuracies that might happen when each party taking part in a transaction maintains its own data set for the transaction. Blocks, including timestamped blocks, serve as the blockchain's data structure by listing aggregated data on transactions that have taken place inside the network. With both financial and non-financial applications effectively applied, blockchain technology is undisputed and has operated without a hitch for years. To learn how retail businesses regard blockchain, we polled a large number of retail professionals as part of this research. The findings are shared and discussed in the parts that follow.

Permissioned and unpermissioned blockchains make up the majority of the market. When using open distributed ledger technology without authorization, the data is shared across a number of machines in the network rather than being owned by a single person or database. Those transaction records are viewable by anyone with network access. The information is timestamped once a transaction is recorded and cannot be changed or removed again. New records or later additions to the ledger are monitored and updated in real-time for all users. Due to its distributed nature, where each copy is present in a distinct location, blockchain is challenging to hack.

Similar to permissioned ones, they can restrict who in the network can authorise transactions. By creating a cryptographic key pair in conjunction with wallet software, a blockchain makes it possible for transactions to be made securely online.

Simple contracts can be created using distributed ledger technology and will be carried out when specific requirements are met. A blockchain project called Ethereum was created with this objective in mind. Although it is still in its infancy, it has the potential to fully use the benefits of blockchain on a worldwide scale.

The retail sector is now driven by data. In order to grow their clientele and enhance customer service, retailers are seeking to concentrate more on personalised retailing.

As an enabler, blockchain technology will help retailers more effectively accomplish their goals. A few of these procedures are mentioned here. In the retail industry, blockchain can assist merchants in enhancing their current business processes, which will spur business growth.

This chapter focuses on a few retail-related situations where blockchain technology can be employed to the advantage of both consumers and retailers. Several components make up the document. The general definitions of Blockchain technology are provided in Section 2, while the evolution of retail supply chain management is covered in Section 3. The main problems with retail supply chain management are covered in Section 3, along with solutions that leverage Blockchain. Section 4 looks into how it might be used in the retail industry, and Section 5 identifies potential difficulties. The paper's sixth and final section is Section 6.

Definition

Blockchain definition has not materially evolved in previous years. Using blockchains, transactions can be recorded in a decentralised and transparent manner (Boucher, Nascimento, & Kritikos 2017). This is the biggest definition, and Lewis may narrow it down even more (2016). He adds that the blockchain maintains a network of databases that are synced amongst various entities, and it records more than simply transactions (Lewis 2016)

However, before becoming the single term it is today, the word blockchain was initially split into two words: block and chain or chain of blocks. These phrases first appeared in “paper Bitcoin of Satoshi Nakamoto: A Electronic Cash System which maintains Peer-to-Peer”. Satoshi Nakamoto, a pseudonym for the person largely regarded as the inventor of Bitcoin and blockchain, wrote the paper under this pseudonym (2017) Bashir There is no precise description of blockchain in Nakamoto's article because it focuses on introducing Bitcoin, a solely peer-to-peer form of electronic cash, and outlining its characteristics. But there are a few important blockchain-related aspects that are discussed. He says that an electronic coin is a chain of digital signatures, which is an indirect definition of chain. Additionally, a group of goods is referred to as a block.

GENERIC ELEMENTS OF BLOCKCHAIN TECHNOLOGY

Transaction

Bashir (2017) defines a transaction as the movement of value from one address (identifier) to another. Information and data not only created and held by users but also information and data owned by other parties are all included in the transferred value. A transaction is the exchange of a digitally recordable asset between two contracting parties, such as data, money, or contracts (Seffinga et al., 2017).

Block

Block A block consists of numerous transactions as well as additional elements like the block hash and date (Bashir, 2017). A fixed-length digital fingerprint or unique identifier is a block hash (hash pointer) (Gupta, 2017). By incorporating the previous timestamp and creating a chain with each new timestamp strengthening the previous ones, the timestamp establishes the data's existence at the time necessary to enter the hash (Nakamoto, 2008).

Node

Depending on its location, a node can perform a variety of activities. In order to foster consensus and protect the blockchain, it is in charge of 15 mining as well as suggesting and authorising transactions. A node may also be assigned validators and straightforward payment verification tasks. (2017) Bashir Among other node types, a network may contain complete nodes and lightweight nodes. The former can store a full local copy of the ledger and process proposed transactions in line with all consensus mechanism criteria, but the latter can only retain a subset of the replicated ledger's data. in Nelson (2017).

Peer-to-Peer Network

One of the essential skeleton's bones that makes up the blockchain is this network topology. As suggested by the name, network peers are able to directly communicate and exchange messages. A peer serves as both a server and a client (requestor) at the same time in order to share resources and have direct access to those of the others (Steinmetz & Wehrle, 2005; The Government of the HKSAR, 2008). RETAIL SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT

Blockchain enables retailers to resolve this customer conundrum and build confidence. How? Each product is given a “digital ID” that secures all of its information from its point of origin to the retail retailer. “At its core, blockchain is a distributed database ledger that uses cryptographic protocols for data sharing, validation, and authentication across a network of nodes”. By maintaining an immutable chain of data, the network enables trust less parties to concur on the existence and state of data stored there. The ever-expanding retail supply chain can be made more efficient and reliable by using blockchain as a platform for mass collaboration and the implementation of collective self-interest.

As you read this, blockchain is still in its early phases and developing. However, there is little doubt that it can enhance the collaboration and transparency of the supply chain. Retailers who can free up their supply chains will be better able to operate efficiently, project a stronger sense of brand value, and deliver a vastly improved consumer experience (www.tcs.com/Unblocking-retail-supply-chain-with-blockchain-1017-1.pdf).

To cut waste, accelerate monitoring, enhance risk prevention, and improve accountability, Walmart is promoting the use of “Blockchain technology in the food supply chain”. The retail behemoth submitted a number of patents pertaining to Blockchain, one of which was for a “Smart Box” system, or a set of apps, that would provide data on a package's contents, environmental circumstances, location, and more. Starbucks is also experimenting with blockchain technology. Pilot projects are being run in Colombia, Costa Rica, and Rwanda to help the business track its “bean to cup” coffee and exchange real-time supply chain information. The major French supermarket chain Carrefour has introduced the first “food Blockchain” in Europe that tracks its animal and vegetable products using the Blockchain technology. Smartphones can be used by consumers to scan QR codes.

Blockchain Supply Chain in Retail

Although the manufacturers seem to be at the top of the supply chain for retailers, many of them are equally worried about the moral standards of their suppliers. This could cover a variety of topics, such as the provenance of the parts that the manufacturer receives, statements about the sustainability of the raw materials, regulatory compliance, waste management, working conditions, and much more.

Regrettably, licenced agencies, foreign distributors, and the brands themselves regularly keep retailers cut off from the manufacturing process. How can they ensure that their suppliers' sustainability and ethical production claims have pleased them and their clients? Currently, this can be done by simply looking at a certificate, which may or may not be authentic.

The legitimacy of raw materials is guaranteed by a blockchain supply chain, supporting claims of fair trade, sustainability, ethical sourcing, and organic production. Additionally, it permits the verification of provenance, giving the battle against fake goods a much-needed boost. This kind of completely interconnected supply chain increases transparency for all parties and enables theoretical planning to be improved with the most recent data without having to wait for the previous stage to be finished.

Transitioning Retail Through Blockchain

The e-commerce revolution began to affect the retail industry in the late 1990s, and retailers who switched from their conventional systems to e-commerce are aware of the potential of disruptive revolutionising technology. The broad range of potential applications for blockchain and the necessary infrastructure modifications will alter the retail industry.

The most significant stakeholder in every retail industry is the consumer, and their trust is both difficult to gain and simple to lose. Blockchain represents a new development in a time when more and more transactions are conducted online. While the retail industry won't be completely transformed by blockchain overnight, there will be enough changes in the next few years to alter the way that retail is currently conducted with deliberate innovation and the right amount of investment.

The adoption of Blockchain technology by retailers can help them greatly with their current business operations, which will help them develop their businesses, according to later sections of the report. Here are a few major areas where this development may be made to help merchants enhance their current business operations, which will promote business expansion. Key Issues in Retail

Changing Consumer Expectation

Consumer expectations are one of the many volatile elements that the retail industry must deal with. In reality, consumer expectations appear to shift quite quickly, making it difficult to keep up. There are simply too many factors at work to change consumer tastes overnight. For example, a large portion of consumers may love a product today, but the next day, they may have different opinions, and some may no longer like the product. Seasonal changes, events, holidays, and trends are all important factors in this. As a result, the retail industry must be astute enough to comprehend all of this information. However, accurate forecasting is still impossible to achieve today.

Retail Price Inflation

These days, consumers must spend an increasing amount for their basic needs. Due to this, individuals frequently have less money available to spend on any luxuries. However, the inconsistent retail prices and large price tags further deter buyers from making purchases. Retailers must thus provide special deals or discounts to get shoppers to buy their goods.

Retail businesses, however, are currently unable to handle the high expense. What gives, though? In other words, improper automation and planning may lead to increased manufacturing costs, which in turn may lead to higher retail pricing.

Ineffective Modern Marketing Strategy

Yes, a lot of retail organisations are increasingly integrating online marketing into their operations. They wind up investing a lot of money, though, with little to no outcomes since they lack the necessary knowledge on the subject. You can sell your products to customers in a variety of methods; you shouldn't restrict yourself to social media.

These days, consumers prefer one-on-one interaction with their personal brands. They might become disinterested in your brand if you can't give them this functionality. Once more, retail businesses may overmarket their goods, which would result in more unhappy customers.

Counterfeit and Forged Goods

One of the biggest problems the industry is facing is the rise in fraud and fake goods. Internal fraud activities also have an effect on income, and there are too many counterfeit goods on the market, which damages the reputation that retail organisations have worked so hard to establish.

Contrary to popular belief, it is getting harder to spot fake goods, which is making customers increasingly angry. Both the client and the retailer will continue to lose money if the problem is not resolved appropriately. Therefore, retailers need to deal with this problem as quickly as feasible.

Cyber Attacks

The growing frequency of cyber-hacks is another obstacle for retailers. The majority of retail establishments really employ the quite insecure client-server networking approach. As a result, breaking into servers and stealing confidential data is a rather simple process. Additionally, since every retailer stores information about its customers, it is comparatively easy to manipulate that information and obtain access to their credit card or bank account details. This might easily turn into a serious security breech, which would cause a huge loss of revenue. Additionally, it suggests that customers are not confident in you with regard to their data, which is bad for your business.

How Blockchain Is Addressing Issues in Retail SCM

Although the financial industry has been successfully using Blockchain technologies for many years, Blockchain technology has the potential to disrupt a variety of other industries such as retail. Some of the advantages of applying blockchain technology in retail supply chain management are as following-

Customer Data Management, Security, and Sharing

Large volumes of client data are regularly registered, stored, and used by retailers. In this area of their work, blockchain applications for simplifying operations represent a less-explored yet very potential topic. Utilizing distributed ledger technology will improve security, allow users more control over their data, and open up new marketing possibilities, assisting merchants in more efficiently meeting customer wants and gaining the value they might have missed otherwise. Retailers will be able to identify the demands of customers and market highly tailored discounts to them with the use of an artificial intelligence-powered recommendation system. Retailers would be able to reward those who have decided to open their data by giving them spendable tokens at the store in exchange for the lowered advertising costs.

By sending retailers shopping lists in the form of smart contracts that make use of the Blockchain data-sharing network, customers can also communicate with them about their wants and needs. Blockchain could serve as the main platform for the future of fully automated shopping when combined with the Internet of Things' potential to assign order execution and distribution to computers.

Transforming Payment

One of the first online merchants to accept Bitcoin payments was Overstock in 2014. Online merchants of all sizes are now accepting cryptocurrency payments, but it will take some time before digital wallets and cryptocurrency payments are widely accepted in the retail industry. The great majority of online shops also frequently accept traditional modes of payment due to the notable fluctuation in bitcoin pricing, while some have found implementation to be too challenging. This implies that the potential of this online payment room is also largely unrealized.

Retailers who are open to experimenting with cryptocurrency payments will open up a new revenue stream and draw in more customers from around the world. A further benefit of blockchain technology is that it allows businesses more control over how their customers distribute and use coupons and discounts. MasterCard, for instance, has applied for a patent for a system that verifies discounts using Blockchain technology. Retailers may more effectively offer highly targeted discounts and avoid coupon abuse thanks to the programme. In order to enhance its programme for rewarding loyal customers, American Express is now experimenting with blockchain technology. The capacity to assist shops speed online payments and reduce fraud is among the most interesting prospective uses for blockchain technology.

Improved Customer Identity Administration

As you are aware, the majority of retail businesses use the very unsafe client-server networking approach. Because of this, it is fairly easy to manipulate that data and obtain the customer's credit card or bank account details. This is a flagrant breach of privacy and a contravention of state law.

Companies in the retail industry can use blockchain to safeguard customer data to solve this problem. In fact, they can authenticate systems and store all data in immutable storage. The customer will only have access to their information as a consequence, and no outsider will be able to hack the system and misuse that information.

Rationalise the Retail Sales Tax

The practise of lowering retail sales tax is another benefit of blockchain in retail. In actuality, sales taxes are an annual requirement for all retail businesses. Many people do, however, attempt to avoid paying this $14.5 billion tax! Additionally, the majority of this tax fraud is committed by internet businesses. Companies could be charged with felonies if this keeps happening.

Blockchain-based automated sales tax collection can help with this problem by helping to collect taxes based on the volume of sales or profit produced. Retailers can also upload their documents, which the network will then verify. This approach is excellent.

Transactions Between Individuals and Merchants

Many retailers are already striving to use this amazing blockchain function. Blockchain can enable person-to-person transactions in a physical store. Actually, both sides gain from the payment procedure. The benefit of taking money directly from the client without utilising any third-party applications is that the customer is not charged more for using other third-party financial services. Additionally, this could promote continued trust between the two parties, which is extremely advantageous for retail businesses.

Reduction in Counterfeit Items

For manufacturers of high-end consumer products, a fall in the price of the upscale good can be caused by the sale of counterfeit goods, which can result in significant losses for the producers and retailers. For this kind of issue, blockchain serves as a straightforward, verified answer. By allowing a blockchain digital ledger record to store all information about every product, including those that are counterfeited, the spread of forgeries can be prevented. Therefore, in these situations, when the end-user receives the package deal of goods, try a code that is totally carved into the product so that you may access all the data stored inside the blockchain's virtual ledger document. retailers vulnerable to product counterfeiting.

Logistics

The same blockchain-based record-keeping tools will make logistics tracking easier and more effective. Logistics experts and customers will be able to inspect and update the blocks that make up your order fulfilment transaction rather than depending on inaccurate and asynchronous databases.

Blockchain-powered logistics is demonstrated by a warehouse employee scanning a tag as they get ready to send a product. The scan on the blockchain provides an immutable record, unlike the initial step in the majority of warehouses today. The manufacturers may have scanned the same tag, updating the same blockchain that you and your customers will read to obtain the same information, if everyone in your ecosystem has access to it. Any node in the supply chain can initiate a smart contract (a programme that operates without the involvement of a human user) by scanning a product, for example, to automatically complete electronic cross-border customs paperwork. A logical outcome of blockchain-based logistics is confidence. People can feel secure knowing that everyone has access to the same information, from the manufacturing plant to the warehouse to your customer's home.

B2B and B2C Smart Contracts

Everywhere you employ software in your retail operation, you should think about transitioning to smart contracts. B2B transactions will be completely automated, and B2C transactions will be able to benefit from a customised experience that is adjusted according to a set of criteria. Smart contracts are the “meat-on-the-bone” of blockchain technology. They'll use previously unheard-of methods to automate the flow of data.

Unlike conventional software, smart contracts can operate without a user's input. These types of B2B and B2C transactions can be automated by using smart contracts, which will assume control and carry out your predefined commands. Some of the most intriguing potential of the blockchain is encapsulated by smart contracts. Engineers might someday replace current huge clouds with these in order to decentralise all data storage. They refer to the seemingly endless possibilities of blockchain and what this technology means for merchants like you now and in the future, knowing that it will be very challenging to forge or trick smart contracts on the blockchain.

Promotions and Vouchers

There's no reason to confine yourself to documents for internal use. Blockchain can also be used to produce coupons and provide discounts for your goods. Again, you may use the security and immutability of the blockchain to more accurately organise your promotional campaigns. You'll be able to calculate the precise effects of each campaign on your business since you'll constantly be aware of how many coupons you have distributed and how many your consumers have utilised. Running your promotions on the blockchain has additional branding advantages. Your coupons will take on a new flavour once your customers realise you are setting a significant forward trend.

Paperless

You will be able to save any warranty you offer with your items as a link to a block on a blockchain rather than producing a physical paper to represent it. To prevent future changes to the file, the external file will have a “checksum” that may be compared to the block.

Going paperless and using it to increase your brand's green credentials would make you feel good knowing that paper demand exceeded 399 million metric tonnes in the previous year. You will also receive the extra benefit of having all of your papers go through the same anti-counterfeiting procedures. You can edit a block to manage your records rather than printing out a piece of paper that can be readily duplicated.

Integrations for Digital and In-Store

By applying the same reasoning, you'll see that you can use blockchain to represent yourself as a forward-thinking shop everywhere you can incorporate it into your physical location or online site. Practically speaking, cross-channel blockchain interfaces will make it simpler to uphold enduring interactions with your clients. Due to the tracking features of blockchain technology, you may first establish a connection with a consumer through your e-commerce platform before realising they are also making purchases from you online. In that instance, you can tailor each customer's online experience based on the learnings from their blockchain data.

Fostering Disintermediation

The Internet “made disintermediation possible and fundamentally altered how firms distribute their goods and services” (Buhalis & Licata, 2002). By eliminating reliance on existing middlemen and creating new types of electronic intermediaries, new technologies have replaced outdated trade practises (Cort, 1999). New online middlemen have also emerged as a result of the Internet, offering a variety of goods and services (McCole, 2004; Pineda & Paraskevas, 2004). The provision of trust is one of the services new e-commerce intermediaries provide.

The popularity of social media has also highlighted how crucial it is for businesses to interact with their clients on platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube. These platforms rely on data and targeted advertisements to make money rather than on user fees for content and services. Furthermore, according to Nieves and Diaz-Meneses (2016), “They have developed a positive feedback loop wherein increased consumer engagement leads in higher expertise and improved content integration.” These digital intermediaries gain the ability to lock businesses and customers onto their exclusive platforms while also assisting them by personalising their brands and offerings.

Changing Customer Profiles

A very country's economic, social, legal, and political changes, as well as most crucially the changes in technology, can result in major changes in the psychographic profile of the customers. Customers' buying behaviours are never static, so it may seem to them that following their behaviour is simple work, but this isn't the case, according to a few research studies by the organisation Project Guru. Today, collecting and preserving such complex and voluminous data is a significant challenge for marketers.

Marketers who work with several stores will implement a blockchain solution. Blockchain technology can be used to create sophisticated information storage systems for retailers because the data stored on the distributed ledger and retrieved through it are both permanent records. This information can then be used to forecast the specific needs of a given neighbourhood, recommend and store enough goods, and improve their just-in-time inventory facility. The amount of information generated in the modern e-commerce world, where same-day and same-hour deliveries are used by all retailers, is enormous. Blockchain serves as the most efficient platform because it can store and retrieve ongoing information, as well as have algorithms that can predict a customer's next purchase. A significant factor is already being produced by the distributed ledger system across its computing network.

Transparency

Customers, retailers, and suppliers can see the data stored in the blockchain and are able to see the product supply, whether or not it was made with child labour, and whether or not there are any harmful or hidden components. These details help retailers and customers make decisions about the product. This blockchain-enhanced openness can more correctly identify client behaviour patterns.

Loyalty

Blockchain will modernise the loyalty programme by securely storing customer information such as coupons and discounts and making it available to all or specific retailers for deeper analytics on customer data. Customers can read all of their loyalty information from all of the retailers in one place thanks to a blockchain loyalty guarantee.

Retail Companies Using Blockchain Technology

Retail customers today are more sceptical and concerned about the veracity of the data offered or the claims made by the seller about the goods. On the other side, it will help the store acquire the consumer's trust if it can give the information or statements in a way that they cannot be disputed. The use of blockchain technology here will be very beneficial. The following businesses are utilising blockchain technology-

Walmart

Walmart is creating blockchain-based retail food traceability systems. For this, they are making use of Hyperledger Fabric. They are now collaborating with IBM to get the necessary technical assistance for the solution. The retail giant has already finished two blockchain proof-of-concept initiatives that were successful. They claim that blockchain can help them maintain food quality and prevent any negative effects.

Amazon

Amazon is making the most of blockchain technology's promise. In their advertising business, they are currently utilising blockchain. Actually, because it can greatly increase their effectiveness, this is an effective use of Blockchain properties. In addition, they offer network creation based on the client's demands when selling Blockchain solutions like Blockchain as a service.

Alibaba

Blockchain-based retail solutions are something else Alibaba is working on. Blockchain technology is being used by the business to enhance product traceability. Additionally, they have already created the Kaola cross-border e-commerce platform on the blockchain. All customs clearances, logistics information, and product registrations will be tracked via this platform. They plan to use it to combat fake goods with a two-dimensional code as a result.

Aldi

Blockchain is being used by Aldi to control its retail supply chain. Currently, they are validating their corporate purchases with technology. With Verifish, they are monitoring Irish seafood that is both sustainable and organic. The project was also developed by Verifish, and the solution is being helped by BIM. The project will last a year, but the company wants to finish it by 2021.

Challenges

Since blockchain technology is still in its infancy, is still at the proof-of-concept stage of development, and few blockchain-based systems have been deployed on an industrial scale, real risks to it may not become apparent for several years until it is more widely employed. This technology should be thoroughly researched before being employed; rash decisions should not be made. Systemic risks could result in catastrophic consequences from failure to implement. As a shared ledger system, blockchain is anticipated to hold sensitive data as well. In order to comply with industry best practises, it must make sure that its encryption and cyber-security are robust. For cloud-based retail solutions, data security and segregation should also be taken into account.

Laws and Standards

Blockchain is currently subject to little or no regulation (Kumar & Mallick, 2018). The adoption of blockchain is facing considerable obstacles from regulations and laws. Without them, supply networks cannot rely on the technology (Kamilaris et al., 2019). Lack of regulation is also problematic because it is unknown how the system should be set up and new rules could be implemented at any time, requiring modifications to the system that has already been established. 2019 (Saberi et al., n.d.) Lack of standards and regulation lead to a diverse range of blockchain implementations with poor interoperability (Tribis et al., 2018; Kesharwani, 2019).

Security

The original blockchain has clear data. Because it was intended to be that way, everyone has access to the data. However, access must be limited because some data may be private for supplier chains. Blockchain does not by default support this, and it is challenging to implement. This has been acknowledged by certain blockchains, like Hyperledger, which has enabled access control (Rabah, 2017; Behnke & Janssen, 2019).

Privacy

Despite being regarded as a very safe technology, blockchain does have some drawbacks. Even while a 51% attack is generally improbable, it has the potential to take over the entire blockchain. It happens when one party takes control of the blockchain by acquiring 51% of the pool's power. The type of power may vary based on the validation technique. For proof-of-work, 51% of processing power would be required (Aliyu et al., 2018; Mohsin et al., 2019). Additionally, blockchain has certain design problems. There is no “getting it back” if you “lose” the private key because it is both too crucial and too light. Users must wait a while before being sure that a transaction has been successfully completed on the blockchain because of the way the nodes communicate.

Adoption

It is challenging to convince parties to cooperate in order to devote time and energy to developing blockchain systems. Despite the fact that it might significantly improve future competitiveness and possibilities, the cost and risk are both substantial (Kesharwani, 2019). Most blockchain technology is experimental and unproven (Rabah, 2017). The creation of new IT tools would be required if blockchain were to be used. Some people in the supply chain might find this challenging (Saberi et al., 2019). In addition, because blockchain has the potential to be a disruptive technology, existing legacy systems may need to be changed or possibly replaced (Saberi et al., 2019).

Management

The success of supply chain practises is largely dependent on top management's support. On the other side, managers might not have the long-term dedication needed to encourage the adoption of new technologies and uphold sustainability.

Lack of knowledge and dedication will jeopardise choices on how to spend money and allocate resources. Adoption of blockchain would be challenging in the absence of proper corporate policies since blockchain could change organisational cultures (Saberi et al., 2019). In addition, blockchain may change how businesses interact and conduct business (Edwards & Chan, 2019). Blockchain will drastically reduce human intervention due to automation and the elimination of intermediaries, which will lead to employment losses. However, adopting blockchain calls for the development of new positions, duties, and knowledge. Everything must be controlled (Saberi et al., 2019; Kamilaris et al., 2019).

RECOMMENDATIONS

Businesses that wish to benefit from blockchain should approach cautiously, according to a Deloitte report. They recommend beginning with “trial projects” that highlight the benefits of blockchain technology for a particular company model. Before using blockchain more broadly, they think it is wise to “experiment, wait, and see.” They advise all business owners to properly design blockchain integrations, but more crucially.

If you are a retailer, you might want to think about creating a loyalty programme that uses blockchain technology or converting an existing loyalty programme to work with a blockchain system. In this manner, you can personally see how blockchain functions within your business model. As you plan your promotional activities, keep in mind the advantages of blockchain technology: you know what you're giving away, no one can fake it, and you represent yourself as a technologically advanced company. This is a win-win situation for your business, and it will probably cost considerably less than you anticipate because the majority of the blockchain technology code is made available under open-source licences on websites like Github. As a retailer, you should also think about how blockchain may affect privacy regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation. In the future, customers may be able to view which businesses have accessed or may access their data thanks to blockchains' ability to store individual data preferences on shared blockchains. Even if this is a longer-term factor, retailers should be aware of it.

CONCLUSION

An economy's foundational component is marketing. In terms of marketing as a function, blockchain technology, which is disruptive, has gotten less attention. Although blockchain has been researched in many different industries, its use in marketing has gotten less attention despite having a lot of potential. In light of the integration of blockchain and marketing that has gaps. The advent of blockchain technology has revolutionised social, financial, and technological developments. Blockchain is now regarded as a reliable and secure technology, despite initially being referred to as a disrupted technology.

As you read this, blockchain is still in its early phases and developing. However, there is little doubt that it can enhance the collaboration and transparency of the supply chain. Retailers with clear supply chains have the chance to boost operational effectiveness, project a stronger brand image, and deliver a vastly improved customer experience.

The blockchain technology was covered in this essay, along with some of its main characteristics and advantages. The technology is still developing, has a wide range of uses across numerous businesses and domains, and is ready to revolutionise the world. It does, however, face several difficulties, some of which have been recognised. Blockchain is the technology that underpins Bitcoin, but it has uses outside of the financial industry. The retail sector will start to benefit from blockchain through increased product transparency, improved supply chain management, a better loyalty management system, improved customer profiling, counterfeiting prevention, and other factors, leading to higher profit margins for retailers and increased customer satisfaction. In 2016, it was discovered that blockchain technology would disrupt the retail sector more than radio frequency identification (RFID).

  • Debasis Mohanty
